content.text:
Paladin spells in DnD 5.5 include iconic options like Divine Smite, as well
	as buffs, healing, and support options, many of which are shared with the
	Cleric’s spell list. They also have a few powerful and unique options like
	Compelled Duel and Find Steed which are rarely available to other classes.

It is tempting for Paladins to dedicate all of their spell slots to Divine
	Smite, but that overlooks many of the Paladin’s most powerful options. Divine
	Smite is certainly both powerful and exciting, but you can do a lot of things
	more interesting than just adding Radiant damage to an attack.
RPGBOT uses a color coding scheme which is simple to understand and easy to read at a glance. This system is designed to help players make informed decisions for their dnd character builds.

items.text:
: Bad, useless options, or options which
		are extremely situational. Nearly never useful.

: OK options, or useful options
		that only apply in rare circumstances. Useful sometimes.

: Fantastic options, often essential
		to the function of your character. Useful very frequently.

content.text: The advice in this article is based on the current
State of the 2024 DnD Character Optimization Meta

as of when the article was last updated. Keep in mind that the state of the meta periodically changes as new source materials are released, and the article will be updated accordingly as time allows. Also be sure to check for
We will not include 3rd-party content, Unearthed Arcnaa content, or homebrew in guides for official content because we can’t assume that your game will allow them.

Fighting Style (Blessed Warrior) allows you to select two Cantrips. In order
	to justify the opportunity cost of choosing Blessed Warrior over any other
	Fighting Style, your choice of Cantrips in the context of the rest of your
	build needs to both justify the opportunity cost and answer the question “why
	not just play a Cleric?”

Since Cantrips reduce your reliance on Strength or Dexterity, Blessed Warrior
	builds will generally be focused on Charisma rather than Strength or
	Dexterity, in which case you should also look for the ability to use Charisma
	for weapon attacks either from taking Magic Initiate (Druid) to get Shillelagh
	or from a level in Warlock to get Pact of the Blade.

items.text:
: Really
		good, but you likely can’t make room for it since you only get two
		Cantrips.

: The
		amount of damage prevented is small and doesn’t scale, so committing
		Concentration to this is hard to justify beyond very low levels. This could
		be useful against low-CR elementals which you’ll face at levels 1 and 2, but
		1d4 damage per turn just isn’t enough beyond that.

: Not as
		much damage as Toll the Dead, and unless you plan to fight a lot of undead,
		and you’ll use both in the same situations, so you can only justify having
		one of the two. Pick the one with better damage.

: 1 point of
		Lay on Hands takes a Bonus Action and will get your target back into a
		fight.

:
		Thematically fun, but not especially useful. See our
Practical Guide to Prestidigitation and Similar Cantrips

: 60 ft.
		range, the damage is measured in d12’s, and since it’s Necrotic damage,
		almost nothing will resist it.

: A
		great way to handle crowds of multiple enemies. Grab full plate and a shield
		and walk into a crowd of enemies. See our article on

for a breakdown of the math comparing melee cantrip spells to normal martial
		attacks.

: If you
		don’t have something else on which to use your Concentration, use Bless.
		+1d4 to attack rolls and saves is huge in 5e.

: This
		is a weird spell. The fact that it exists implies that spellcasters perform
		burial rites, wedding ceremonies, and rites of passage magically at a cost
		of 25gp each.

It certainly feels cool to have a dedicated mechanic for performing these
			functions, but I don’t know why this isn’t just a Religion check or
			something. It also creates a bizarre economic divide because of the 25gp
			price tag between people who can and can’t afford to blow that gold on
			making a religious ceremony literally magic.

Regardless of all of that, the spell provides weird incentives to do
			things like getting married before a dungeon crawl or a boss fight. As a
			DM I would discourage players from abusing these options.

: Useful,
		but only effective if you’re building around Charisma.

: Forcing
		a foe into single combat with you is extremely helpful. You are likely your
		party’s Defender, and while much of the time that only requires you to stand
		in the right place, sometimes you will need to actively force enemies to
		attack you instead of your allies.

: Use lay
		on hands. You don’t get enough spell slots to spend them on healing.

:
		Situationally useful, and you can use it to find invisible enemies or detect
		enemies through thin walls.

: Someone
		in the party needs this, and ideally it should be someone with the ability
		to cast rituals.

: Very
		situational, and unless you can also cast Protection From Poison there’s
		little you can do about it anyway. Fortunately, this can be cast as a
		ritual, but you can’t do that so leave it to someone who can.

: 1d4
		damage on hit, Bonus Action casting time, no Concnetration. While it’s
		certianly not as exciting as Divine Smite, four hits with this running deals
		as much damage as level 1 Divine Smite, and Divine Favor lasts for a full
		minute. If you’re expecting a long fight, if you’re using two weapons (or
		Polearm Master), or if you have Extra Attack, this is likely a more
		efficient use of a level 1 spell slot.

: The
		damage is good and the scaling is good, but this doesn’t get you anything
		except damage. It’s a perfectly fine spell, and it’s a great baseline to
		measure other Paladin spells against.

: A truly
		fantastic buff for a level 1 spell, but you’re going likely be the one who
		needs this most since Paladins are typically the party’s Defender, and
		Concentration will make the spell difficult to rely upon. Shield of Faith is
		better damage mitigation and has a Bonus Action casting time, so it’s nearly
		always a better choice.

: A
		fantastic defensive buff, and even though it requires Concentration it will
		be reliable between Disadvantage on attacks against you and your high AC
		while stomping around in heavy armor.

: One of
		many reasons that Dungeons and Dragons makes a terrible wilderness survival
		game. Leave this for someone who can cast rituals if possible.

: You are
		guaranteed 2d6 fire damage, and you get more if your target fails their
		save. You get 1d6 per spell level immediately, then another 1d6 per spell
		level at the start of each of the target’s turns for up to a minute. The
		scaling is also better than Divine Smite, adding a total of 2d6 per spell
		level compared to Divine Smite’s 1d8 per spell level.

Of course, there are still problems here. Constitution saves are
			typically high, so enemies are unlikely to fail the save, so you can only
			count on the initial two instances of damage. Even if you’re building
			around Charisma, you can only count on that initial damage, and anything
			beyond the target’s next turn is a pleasant surprise. Fire resistance and
			immunity are common, so the damage type is also worse than Divine Smite.
			Finally, there is some value in Divine Smite immediately dealing damage
			compared to waiting for the target’s turn, especially if the damage
			reduces the target to 0.

: Not
		very exciting, and it takes Concentration, but a paladin with full plate, a
		shield, Defense fighting style, and Shield of Faith has an AC of 23, which
		will keep you very safe for a very long time.

: You
		only lose 2 damage on average compared to Divine Smite, and pushing enemies
		away and knocking them Prone is easily worth the lost damage if your party
		is going to capitalize on the target being Prone before they can stand
		again.

If you combine this with the Push Weapon Mastery, you can knock enemies a
			total of 10 feet away. A creature with 30 ft. speed would then spend half
			to stand, walk 15 feet, and still be 5 feet too far away from you, meaning
			that they may be unable to attack you that turn.

: A
		weaker version of Tasha’s Mind Whip, Wardaway makes some huge trades to fit
		into a level 1 spell. The damage is obviously much worse, but that’s not why
		you’re here. The target still gets to move and act in the same turn, but
		halving their speed is still impactful. The biggest limitation is that
		Wardaway uses a Constitution save instead of a much more reliable
		Intelligence save.

At low levels where enemies have very few saving throw proficiencies,
			Wardaway may be decently reliable. But enemies at low levels also rarely
			have Bonus Actions, so they’re likely to fail the save and barely notice
			the spell’s effect.

: You
		trade a considerable amount of Divine Smite’s damage for an excellent
		debuff. Frightened enemies can’t willingly move closer to the source of
		their fear, so you can use the Push Weapon Mastery to push enemies out of
		reach and leave them unable to get back into melee until the condition
		ends.

: Not
		essential, but a good way to pad your party’s hit points throughout the day.
		Just be careful; if the spell ends while you’re below 5 hit points you’ll
		fall to 0 and fall unconscious.

Aid’s casting time allows it to be used in combat, which is unusual but
			offers an interesting option. With three targets and a 30-foot range, you
			can cast it to both buff and heal your allies during combat. Targets
			current hit points and hit point maximum both increase, so allies at 0 hit
			points are healed in addition to having their hit point maximum raised,
			thereby allowing Aid to serve a similar function to Mass Healing Word.

However, since spells don’t stack with themselves, it’s hard to repeat
			this trick. You’ll need to cast Aid again using higher-level spell slots,
			which can get expensive quickly, so Mass Healing Word is probably better
			if Aid is already running and if Mass Healing Word is an option for your
			party.

: More
		plot point than actual spell, this will rarely see use by players in a
		typical campaign. Used as intended, this creates a small area in which two
		characters can kick each other in the shins until someone runs out of hit
		points without risk of anyone actualy dying. But it doesn’t do anything
		about other nasty effects, so participants can petrify, curse, or otherwise
		ruin their opponent’s day without Dueling Ground protecting them.

Dueling Ground’s fighting ring is notably porous. The participants are
			free to interact with anything outside of the ring unless they leave it,
			and even then the spell doesn’t actually end. If you can bring this up in
			time for combat, you can effectively give both participants Death Ward for
			the spell’s duration (or until a third creature enters the area).

: Find
		Steed gives you a magical mount and addresses some my many problems with
		5e’s

Among the steed’s many benefits, its hit points scale with spell level, so
		it gets more durable as enemies’ attacks get more dangerous. This means that
		you can actually expect the steed to survive more than a single hit.

: Very
		situational, but it solves some interesting problems. Normally you can
		cremate a body to prevent it from becoming undead, but cremating a body
		takes an alarmingly large amount of fuel which you probably don’t have
		laying about. You can mutilate the body, but that’s gross and in many
		campaign settings the gods view that sort of thing as evil. So if you need
		to maintain a body until you can give it a real burial, this is your best
		bet.

Gentle Repose also pauses the timer on effects which raise the dead.
			While this is specifically called out as working with Raise Dead, it works
			with anything that raises creatures from the dead. That includes Revivify.
			So if you keep this prepared, you can haul your allies around until you
			can cast 3rd-level spells and until you can scrape together enough diamond
			dust to raise them.

Remember that while spells don’t stack, their durations can overlap so if
			you cast Gentle Repose early to avoid gaps in spell duration you can keep
			bodies preserved indefinitely.

:
		Situational, but a situation that comes up often. If you don’t have a cleric
		in the party you may be the only one with access to this spell, so you’ll
		want to take it at some point.

: Too
		situational, and too easy to counter. Anyone with any knowledge of magic
		that’s trying to hide something will wrap it in lead.

: If your
		game uses magic items, you may never need this. If it doesn’t, this is
		essential. A bonus to your attacks makes your damage output multiplicatively
		more reliable. With a 1-hour duration and no Concentration, one casting
		provides a lot of value from one of your few spell slots.

: A Short
		Rest plus some extra healing for 5 targets. Useful if you’re pressed for
		time or if your party goes through hit points quickly and needs more healing
		than Hit Point Dice can provide.

:
		Situational, but poison is common across the full CR range, so this is a
		fantastic defensive option at any level. The 1-hour duration means that you
		can get a lot of mileage out of a single spell slot even if you cast it
		ahead of time.

: The
		damage is dismal, but you’re here for the debuff. Unfortunately, Con saves
		ten to be high, so many enemies will be able to reliably pass the save. If
		you manage to catch a crowd of enemies (probably 3 or more), it may be worth
		the gamble.

: Only
		situationally useful, but very important if your party doesn’t have another
		counter to hidden or invisible enemies. The DnD 5.5 stealth rules use the
		Invisible condition for hidden creatures, so this outright prevents stealth.
		Against creautre sthat use actual invisibility, you can cast this after you
		hit them and then you’re good as long as you can maintain Concentration.

: Few
		characters are so well-suited to use this spell as the Paladin. With d10 hit
		dice and Lay on Hands you have a huge well of hit points, and using this
		provides a great deal of protection to comparably fragile allies. This also
		doesn’t require Concentration, so you can combine it with options like
		Heroism to further mitigate damage.

:
		Situational and much less reliable than you would hope. Creatures are aware
		that they’re under the effect, and they can choose to “be evasive”, which
		means that they could give you true but useless answers or simply not
		answer. Creatures other than the caster also don’t know who passed or failed
		the save, so unless they already trust you other creatures might not believe
		you when you tell them that a creature is telling the truth.

If a creature is willing to talk, they can prove that they are saying
			what they believe to be true, and you can know whether or not they believe
			it to be true. But if the creature is incorrect, if you’re lying to other
			creatures (which they might believe that you are), or if any other number
			of other things go wrong, this spell simply fails to meet its intended
			purpose.

In short, this helps honest creatures prove to you that they are being
			honest. Nothing else. If you want to get answers from an unwilling or
			unhelpful subject, cast Detect Thoughts.

: Never
		use this in combat, but 20d6 healing for a level 3 spell is very efficient.
		That’s an average of 70 hit points, which matches Heal.

: Compared to Divine
		Smite, you lose 1d8 damage to potentially

the target. That’s a really good trade even if the blindness only lasts for
		one round. Constitution saves are high, but you’re gambling 1d8 damage to
		blind a creature likely for an entire encounter with no way to recover, so
		it’s worth the gamble.

: Rations
		are cheap, but it’s good that you can prepare this if you somehow find
		yourself somewhere without food for extended periods. This also lets you
		create 30 gallons of water, which is enough for a nice bath but not enough
		to fill a 5-foot cube.

: Divine Favor, but for
		yourself and all of your allies within 30 ft. It gets better in larger
		parties, especially if you have allies who make lots of attacks, such as by
		using two weapons, Polearm Master, Action Surge, or Flurry of Blows. 1d4
		damage ism’t a lot, so your party really needs to make a lot of attacks to
		justify this.

: A
		Continual Flame, Light, or even a torch is typically sufficient, but
		sometimes you need to light up larger areas like dark battlefields or
		massive caverns. This also dispels magical darkness of 3rd level or lower,
		which is great if you’re fighting enemies like drow which can produce
		magical darkness. Tragically, you can’t cast Daylight at a higher level to
		dispel magical darkness of higher levels.

: Useful, but you get
		this so much later that your party should have access to this from a full
		spellcaster.

: Not
		significantly better than Magic Weapon, a spell level higher, and it takes
		Concentration. Unfortunately, you can’t use both. Instead, you can cast
		Magic Weapon and Divine Favor to get the same attack bonus and the same
		amount of additional damage.

: Situational, but
		irreplaceable. Fortunately, you can usually wait a day to prepare this.

: Too good to forgo.
		Everyone who can get this should take it.

: With a 1-minute
		duration and a Bonus Action casting time, this is a linear upgrade from
		Divine Favor. You upgrade from 1d4 to 1d8 damage, and you can impose a -10
		speed penalty on nearby enemies. Stack that with a Slow weapon and
		potentially the Slasher feat, and you can potentially drop an enemy’s speed
		to 0.

We can also do a basic damage comparison with Divine Smite. A level 3
			Divine Smite deals 4d8 damage. Combat is expected to take roughly 3
			rounds, and you have Extra Attack by this level. If you hit with 4 of your
			6 attacks in those three rounds, Spirit Shroud will do the same amount of
			damage. Divine Smite will still be more impressive on crits, but Spirit
			Shroud is more consistent and is much more useful beyond just damage.

: Only useful if you know
		that you’re facing the types of undead which reduce your hit point maximum
		(there are several).

: Technically
		situational, but the defenses are broad enough that you can cover a wide
		variety of situations. In most encounters it’s unlikely that you’ll be hit
		with more than one or two negative status conditions, but Aura of Purity
		provides broad enough protection that you’ll be able to counter many of the
		most common conditions with the same spell.

: A great way to remove
		an enemy from a fight. Many creatures have poor Charisma saves well into
		high levels, so even a Paladin with middling Charisma may be able to use
		this reliably. It’s tempting to drop this once you can cast Banishing Smite.
		Don’t.

: This will absolutely
		save your life, and with an 8 hour duration you can cast it at the beginning
		of the day before you go do anything dangerous.

: A curious leftover
		from the 2014 rules, Find Greater Steed is still allowed since it hasn’t
		been reprinted. The allowed creatures include options with fly speeds, but
		the DnD 5.5 version of Find Steed will give you a much more durable steed
		since its hit points will scale.

: More
		effective than mundane tracking, but the 1,000-foot range can be a problem
		if the target is actively fleeing from you. If you’re going to use this, be
		sure that you’re moving faster than your target.

: You
		trade much of Divine Smite’s damage for a 1-round save-or-suck. Stunned will
		break Concentration, and the target can’t do anything on their turn except
		move. You might follow this by shoving and/or grappling your target while
		they have Disadvantage on Strength and Dexterity saves.

: Roughly the same damage
		as a level 5 Divine Smite, plus the added banishment effect. Unfortunately,
		the banishment effect isn’t great. The target needs to be below 50 hp after
		the spell’s damage is applied, and then the target still gets a Charisma
		save. The only advantage compared to Banishment is that Banishing Smite has
		a Bonus Action casting time.

: Technically
		situational, but spellcasting enemies are common at such high level.

: This is a decent AOE
		for a class that otherwise struggles to handle groups of foes since Paladins
		don’t get any other area damage spells. 10d6 damage is a big pile, and the
		damage types are very rarely resisted. Unfortunately, it’s on a Con save, so
		you need to expect that enemies will pass the save.

: In most cases,
		Protection from Evil and Good will do the trick, but Dispel Evil and Good
		has two additional effects. You can prematurely end the spell to end a
		charm/frighten/possession effect, or to attempt to banish creatures from
		other planes. They do still get a saving throw, and if the creatures are
		native to the plane they’re on, nothing happens.

It’s very important to note that the banishment effect isn’t limited by
			the spell’s duration: creatures banished this way are sent to another
			plane and must return by normal means. However, since the banishment
			effect doesn’t affect creatures on their home plane, the banishment is
			usually not as appealing as the spell Banishment, which can affect
			creatures native to your current plane. The one advantage is that you
			don’t need to maintain Concentration for the spell’s 1-minute duration for
			your target to remain on their home plane.

: This spell is
		situational by design. It has a 1-minute casting time and Verbal components,
		so you’re not going to break this out in combat or while sneaking around in
		a dungeon. You’re going to restrain the subject, and stand around chanting
		for a full minute and hope that they fail the save. Once that’s done, you
		need to give them a suitable command (read the spell description). Generally
		you’ll want it to be something that benefits you, but will also take the
		target most of the duration to keep them from becoming a problem for you.
		Also remember that the base effect of the Charmed condition makes it easier
		for you to talk the creature into doing things with Charisma checks, so a
		Geased creature may be a useful ally for the duration of the effect even if
		the original order isn’t directly related to what you want them to do.

Increasing the spell level extends the duration, but weirdly the damage
			doesn’t increase. 5d10 is a nice pile of damage, but it doesn’t scale with
			spell level and at some point the target will get smart enough to wake up,
			trigger the 5d10 damage, take a short rest, then go about their business.
			If the damage scaled this would be less of a problem, but damage is so
			easily repaired in 5e outside of combat that without further penalties
			Geas is more a tax on hit dice than the magical shackles it’s intended to
			be.

If you want a homebrew fix, add a level of fatigue each day that the
			target is out of compliance, or make the damage impossible to heal until
			they go a day without taking it. Neither of those is a perfect solution,
			but they’re miles better than an average of 27.5 damage.

: If you
		don’t have a Cleric in the party, you need this.

: An excellent damage
		boost. +2d8 radiant damage on hit means that you’re doing as much damage as
		you would do by burning a low-level spell slot to use Holy Smite. Your
		weapon becomes a magic weapon so you can bypass many creatures’ damage
		reduction. You get all of this for an hour with Concentration, and you can
		cast it as a Bonus Action. You can also dismiss the spell for a cool burst
		of damage, but that’s probably not going to see a lot of use unless the
		duration happens to run out while you’re fighting.

The most direct comparison is to level 5 Spirit Shroud. Spirit Shroud
			will add the same amount of extra damage plus the slow effect on nearby
			enemies, but Spirit Shroud only lasts 1 minute. On a class that gets
			exactly one level 5 spell slot, you really want to get a lot of mileage
			out of it, so Holy Weapon’s 1-hour duration is much more appealing.

: Essential, but by this
		level you should have access to Raise Dead already from other spellcasters
		in the party.

(Optional): The
		Paladin’s best level 5 spell in combat. While your summon won’t be as
		effective as that of full caster, it’s still very good. Two attacks that do
		as much damage as the damage boost from Holy Weapon, plus a powerful rider
		effect and another body on the field to block space and make Opportunity
		Attacks.

Unfortunately, the summon’s attack bonus uses your spell attack modifier.
			Unless you have 20 Charisma (which you might by this level even if you’re
			not doing a Charisma-focused build), the summon’s relatively unreliable
			attacks may be a problem depending on exactly what your spell attack
			modifier is.
